Bounar, Sunday.—The reports brought by native. to Generals Sondem and Phayre are of a nature greatly to allay the fears that have been excited as to the mfety of General Bartow'. force. The battle le said to hove been well con- tested. The British cavalry and artillery were badly cut UP at the commencement of the battle, but the infantry billickd each heavy lose upon Avnob's army that it has not ventured to advance upon Cando., General Barrows in said to have reached Candshar with his infantry. div.p: THE EXAMINER
SATURDAY AUGUST 7. MR

The Compersation Disturbance (Ireland) Bill has met the fate we anticipeted it would do in the House of Lords. After discnenteg the measure for two eighte the Peers rejected its eirond reading by 281 to 51 votes. We very much question whether for • genera- Mon at beet the members of the Upper Chamber have, on any single ocaceirm, assembled in such large numbers as they did on Tueeday evening in their gilded chamber. Where the carrion is there will there will the eaglm gather is a proverb as old ea the hills, and the members of the landowners department of the Legislature, with a keener interest in their hereditary elms privileges than in the raireesing of wrong and ; the promotion of the public weal, have this week mustered in each tome, and evinced inch an anima- . ties, that the event will stand out as • prominent epoch in the history of the usually lethargic Howie of Peen. div.head: IMISSION F NOXIOUS (USE AT ST. HELENS. PROSECUTION OF CHEMICAL MANUFACTURERS
div.p: THE IMISSION F NOXIOUS (USE AT ST. HELENS. PROSECUTION OF CHEMICAL MANUFACTURERS

BY THE LOCAL WOVERNMENT BOAED. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wedtwelay last, I before T. P. E. Thompson, Esq , judge, and epecial jury. catie rams up for hearing in which Dr. Robert Angus Smith, chief inspector of chemical works, en., under the Alkali Arts, brought an action to recover from William Chadwick end Thomas Chadwick, both of Mancheeter, and Joefet Wycliffe Kynaston, of St. Helens, all trading under the name or nom of the ht. Hekos Chemical Company, at Pocket Nook. a penalty alleged to have been incurred by them under the provisions of the Alkali Act, 1N63. M. Bradbury, berritter, of Manchester (instructed by Messrs. Itarbyekire end Tatham, of Manchester,) prosecuted on be- half of the Local.Gove:nment Board; and Mr. Swift, solicitor,

St. Helens, defrosted the company. Mr. Bradbury, tn opening the case, SAt.t the action wall brought under an Act of Parliarnent whereby people who carried on works which gave offenaive discharges were liable to be prosecuted. The action was taken by the Local Government Board, for who I, Smith acted es inspector. It was well known the in the 'notes, of manufacturing chemicals certain gams. harmful and annoying, were given aft and as early n INS an Act of Parliament was paned which regulated the way in which these work. were to be carried on. That Ad allowed a certain proportion of nazi.cd gas called mnriatic acid gas to be given off. He had no doubt the sections 01 that Act would be familiar to the learned
Jd I am afraid not. I do not remember having a camp( thiaaort befota..
Mr. Bradbury I think your Honour has had eases of this sae.t.beforer in. fact, I remionlicr one as far back .1877
M. Swiltl My o'ven imprea.iott corroborates that of Mr. Bradbury's. 1 thiuk sou base adjudicated a similar ease before?

His Henour Was there a jury? Mr. Bradbury There was and the same defendants were the people summoned at that time. flit may have forgotten the circumstance. Mr. Bradbury, continuing, said the Act relating to alkali works provided niacin the manufacture of alkali only 3 cer- tibia proportion of gas ehould be given off. The fourth dection of the Act passed in 1882 provides "That in the manufacture of alkali if the manufacturer does not condense at least 95 per cent, of the muriatic gas evolved in the works and p.issing into the atmosphere, he shall conclusively be taken to be guilty of an ea.., under the section and be liable for the Brat offence to a penalty not exceeding £5O, and for the second offence to a penalty not excteding .C 100. A later Act was pissed in 1874, which amended the foregoing and provided that net only ohall the manufacturer condense 05 per cent. of tbe muriatic acid gas, hot provided that in addition to the condensation of such percentage the works , eh,uld be carried 00 10 each a manner as to secure conden• station (to the satisfaction of the inspector, or sub-inspector, ' as derived from his own eo iminotion) of the muriatic acid gas evolved in each works, to such an extent that in each cubic foot of air, smoke, or chimney gases there shall oaths more than one-fifth part of a grain :4 °lunatic acid gas that escapee into the atinosphere. The defendants were charged for that they slid allow to escape into the atmosphere muriatic acid gas that containe.l more than one- fifth of a grain to every cubic foot of air. The eection to his mind meant that when the offence was proved there WAS AU end to thequestion. There woe no need for the prosecution to piked negligence at all. It woe for the defendants of all coma land all peril to prevent a greater AM.. of niuriatic acid I gas than® per cent escaping into the atmosphere, and that wren perfectly eau thing to do. All he bad to do was to satisfy the jury that an offence had been coinmitted, and then it War for them to ray what penalty should he inflicted. He had no doubt that Parliament in pluming that Act took great care to fin the limit at such a point that the gas could be easily kept below it, and it was the duty of the defendants In keep below the standard frail by Parliatnent. It was rather as anomalous position for a jury to be placed in, namely, to say what amount of penalty shall be indicted for the offence committed. Ile knew of no Act of Parliament where a jury were appointed to give sentence and say how a person should be punished. His Honour : Are there :toy decisions upon this point ? /dr. Swift No, your Honour. His Honour Iheause 1 shall have to advise the jury on the point. It is turning • civil court into • .073 of criminal jurisdiction. I never heard of snare where a jure hail lit nay what penally should to indicted. _ .• . .

Mr. Sift: Tiler ACT-'of-Parliarstent expressly puts it upon LIM footing of a debt. His Honour: ire; but in the Pharrnaceirtical Acts, end , 1 others of a like naturr, the penalties are fixed. Mr. Bradbury cantintring Lis address to the jury) said that they were not put in the position a jury ordinarily 00- copied, for if they found the defendants guilty they had to wiy what puniehment should be inflicted for breaking the !law. He might say that Dr Smith had no vindictivenew in I I the matter, but was simply discharging his duty, end it lay ,in their hands whether the Act of Parliament should be carried out, or •hether tbe defendants shiwki be allowed tx carry ou the practice with impunity, anti infringe a provision, , which you a valuable one to the cominunity, Isecruse there , was no doubt about it that the gasts emitted by the Men. dents and similar works were highly injurious to vegetation land human life. If jurymen looked upon auch cases with a favourable eye it would he an unfortunate thing for the community. Tat W. the third time in which people carrying an works in St. Helens had been before the court, anal in 1877 the same defendants were c ineictid ant pre- cisely similar charge to that with which they stood indicted Chef day. Allred Evans Fletcher sworn, said he lined at Edgebill, Liverpool, and was 0(.8A-inspector for that district under the Alkali Ants. On the 4th June he visited the cefendantre works in order to feet the quantity of gas emitted. lie nude his test in the usual way, namely. by inserting a glass the into a hole prepared in the aide of thV chimney, and with- drawing therefrom a cubic foot of euroke. On teeing it aftgsvards he found the muriatic acid gas to amount to 26-100 of • grain to the cubic foot. Witnras made the analysis in the preeence of 000.1 C of the defendants, and they knew the result at the time. . .
That being the evidence for the prosecution, Mr. Swift said he would roll his witnewes before addressing the jury for the defence.

—lie-o-rg-e—in-rdikin said he was the manager of the Pocket Nook Chemical Works. He bad been employed there for four months. Ile telnembeiid the visit of Dr. Fletcher. and I if there had beon any improper escape of gas he should have heard of it. He afterwards went to wie Dr. Fletcher at the laboratory, and told hint he was surprised ttt hear that the chimney was bad, as the plant was in excellent order. Ile then ilrew witnota's attention to a leakage in olle of the acid troughs, and said that that would cocoon t for the extra amount of gas in the chimney. One of the stones that formed the sides of the cistern was crackcl, but he had never noticed it before. Ile told in. Fletcher that he had been round the works several times that morning, and the leakage did not exist when be viNitof each time. ""• " • "
Mr' Oaskell (foreman of the jurp wanted to know how far the trough would be from the chimney.

Witness ;aid it would be about thirty .iards. Mr. Swift (addressing the Jury for the tlefence) said that the learned counsel for the prosecution awinned that the only duty which thy hod to perfortn was to fix the ammmt ,of penalty to be impored upon the defen tonto. He took it for granted that the offence bait been committed, and that they had merely to as,ese the damages, but he might tell them that was not the only cpiestion for them to decide. .Piret of all, had an offence been committed, and, EPC.,ndly, If an offence had been committed, what wit tl e penalty to he? First of all had there been an offence committed He might call their attention to an Act of Parliament a section of which had been brought under their notice. That day they had nothing to do with the Off pet cent. alluded to by the learned counrel because a eubsequent net had been petard establishing an alternative method of ascertaining the atnount of excess. That section of the Act read as follows The owner of any alkali works in which any offence against the hew had been proved to be committed, and for which a pecuniary penalty may be imposed, stall in every case be deemed to have committed the offence, and shall he liable to pay a penalty entree there shall he proved to the satisfaction of the court that there has been need all due diligence to comply with and deface the ex,eution of this act, and that the office in queetion we, conimitted by some agent, eervant. or workinan, who shall be charged by name as the actnal offender. without the master s coneent or con- nivance, in which case tech agent, servant, or workman shall he liable to be lined for the payment of the p.nalty." Under that Actor Parliament it war quite clear that they must he satbEed that an offence had been committed, and it clearly (Mowed that if a workman committed the offence the nits.. was exonerated from all blame. He had proved that the excess of gas had been the reault of a mushy, and therefore the offence had beim committed in the c..;erving out of the wwk, and an accident over which they had no control, and for which they ought net to be stamped an offender.. It Wan very natural that a crack might occur in the cinern and allow gee to escape, and it was a Null foe which they were not to blame. It was an accident no one could foresee, and for which no one was answerable, but if the jun did think that the defendants were liable to some extent then he asked them that under the circumstances only a stnal I penalty should he inflicted. His Honour, in maiming up the am to the jury, pointed out that the defendants did not attempt to dispute that there had been en escape of gee front their works, and HIM they rendered therneelves liable to a penalty rot exceeding LIOO. If Hey came to the conclueion that the excessive ene.Epe of gas no. due to mirelegeness, then they most take . into ewaideratiew that the defendante had previously been lined Ices similar offence, but if they believed that the erc.spe of gas wand ... to a midden accident to the plant, then they each not to let the tact that the dchnlants bed been . previeuely convicted affect their minds in coming to the concl 41111011 AS to what amount of penalty should be imposed., The jury retired to consider hoet verdict, and on their re- appeatamw the for.tuan sant that they found that an offtnice , had been committed, and Hat a PormEY tes indieted. snarled with a attoow recommendation tlmt • nab-inspector of the Lecal Government Board should In rerident in St. Helen, front the fact that noxious gases are emitted by other works as much if MS more time the defeadaum in Hie Coo. and that In:twines gases are often emitted in At. Helens when ihoot possible Inc the sub.i.verr, who live. at Edge 11111, to be conansuicated with in time.
